## 1 Kings 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview & Context

Elijah bursts onto the scene without genealogy or introduction. His name means "Yahweh is my God"—a declaration itself against Baal worship. The chapter covers three episodes: the drought announcement and hiding at Cherith (vv. 1–7), the widow of Zarephath and the miraculous flour and oil (vv. 8–16), and the raising of the widow's son (vv. 17–24). Jesus Himself cited the Zarephath episode to show God's freedom to bless Gentiles (Luke 4:25–26).

— **Ellicott**: Chapter 17 "contains the one scene of domestic affection and rest in the stormy career of Elijah." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Constable**: Notes a chiastic structure spanning chapters 17–19, with the drought announcement (17:1), journey from Israel (17:2–5), two encounters (ravens, widow), and miracle of resuscitation as parallel to later fire and theophany. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)

---

### v. 1 — Elijah's Dramatic Entrance and Drought Pronouncement

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah appears suddenly ("like a meteor flashing across the darkened sky" — John Whitcomb, cited at Precept Austin). He confronts Ahab with an oath: no dew or rain except at Elijah's word. This is a direct assault on Baal, the Canaanite storm/fertility god. Elijah's phrase "before whom I stand" marks him as one conscious of standing in God's presence even while standing before a king—Gabriel uses similar language (Luke 1:19).

— **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** David Guzik says Elijah "showed the source of his strength… Everyone else felt that the LORD was dead, but for Elijah the LORD lived." The drought was aimed at Baal, the supposed sky god. Elijah "was not merely the prophet of this drought — in the sense of prayer — he was the cause of the drought" (citing James 5:17). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill (Baptist, older):** Gill notes Elijah "swears by the living God, in whose presence he was… standing was a prayer gesture." He reads "according to my word" as referring to prayer: "it was at the prayer of Elijah that rain was withheld." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Desiring God / John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Piper teaches that Elijah prayed according to God's Word — specifically Deuteronomy 11:16–17, where God promised drought as punishment for idolatry. "Elijah is simply claiming the promise of God's word." Before confronting Ahab at the palace, Elijah had been on his knees: "Because he knew of the real King, before whom he stood, he did not fear standing before this mere mortal." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/learning-from-an-insane-prayer-life)
— **Precept Austin (Evangelical, compiles multiple sources):** Notes that "the phrase 'except by my word' is interesting and it might sound like presumption." Elijah knew God's will from Deuteronomy and had prayed earnestly. Also cites F.B. Meyer: "The old religion against the new; the child of nature against the effeminate child of the courts; camel's hair against soft clothing; moral strength against moral weakness." Philip Ryken: "The fear of God had driven out Elijah's fear of man." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-17-commentary)
— **Pulpit Commentary / Ellicott (Anglican):** Ellicott describes Elijah as "simply a warrior of God, bearing witness for Him by word and by deed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/17.htm)

**Traditions Compared:** Most Protestant traditions agree on v. 1. The Reformed/Baptist emphasis (Piper, Ryken) stresses that Elijah prayed Scripture-based prayers. Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik) stresses the power of the prophet's spoken word. Both see the drought as a direct challenge to Baal.

---

### v. 2 — The Word of the LORD Comes

**Traditional Reading:** A "revelation" (literally "word") from the LORD comes to Elijah immediately after his confrontation — God intervenes to protect His prophet.

— **Gill:** "The word of prophecy, as the Targum; this shows that by word, in the former verse, he means the word of the Lord by him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)

---

### vv. 3–4 — Hide at the Brook Cherith; Ravens to Feed You

**Traditional Reading:** God commands Elijah to hide eastward by the Brook Cherith (a wadi flowing into the Jordan). God promises water from the brook and food brought by ravens. This is both protection (from Ahab's wrath) and training in dependence.

— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "God led Elijah one step at a time. He did not tell him to go to Cherith until he first delivered the message to Ahab." God taught Elijah "the value of the hidden life" at his moment of fame. The name Cherith comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to cut away" — God had cutting and refining to do. Cites F.B. Meyer: "We must not be surprised, then, if sometimes our Father says: 'There, child, thou hast had enough of this hurry, and publicity, and excitement; get thee hence, and hide thyself by the brook.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill:** Notes the danger to Elijah "from Ahab and Jezebel, provoked by his reproofs, threatenings, and prophecies." Regarding "ravens" (`orebim`), Gill rejects alternative interpretations (angels, Arabs, merchants, inhabitants of a city called Oreb): "it seems better to interpret them of ravens, as we do, these creatures delighting to be in solitary places." The ceremonial uncleanness was "dispensed with in an extraordinary case." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Ellicott / Pulpit (Anglican):** The Pulpit Commentary strongly defends the literal raven reading against revisionist interpretations: "The singularly prosaic interpretations… such as 'Arabs,' 'merchants'… seem to have arisen simply from a desire to get rid of what seemed a strange miracle, at the cost of substituting for it a gross improbability." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Constable (Dispensational):** "Ravens do not even feed their own young (cf. Job 38:41). God provided miraculously for Elijah to build the prophet's faith in view of the conflicts he would face." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)

---

### v. 5 — Elijah's Immediate Obedience

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah obeys without hesitation — "he went and did according to the word of the LORD."

— **Gill:** "Took his journey eastward, and hid himself in the place directed to." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Precept Austin:** Quotes J.R. Miller: "Elijah defines his relation to God in the phrase, 'before whom I stand.' He meant that he was God's messenger, always standing before God's face, ready to go instantly on His errands. He never sat down in God's presence — but always stood, girded and sandaled, ready for immediate running." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-17-commentary)

---

### v. 6 — Ravens Bring Bread and Meat Twice Daily

**Traditional Reading:** Ravens brought bread and meat morning and evening — a miraculous provision echoing the manna in the wilderness. Elijah had to accept food from unclean animals, learning to prioritize the spirit of the law over its letter.

— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Every bit of food that came to Elijah came from the beak of an unclean animal. Elijah had to put away his traditional ideas of clean and unclean or he would die of starvation." Quotes Spurgeon: God may bring a good word through an unclean vessel, and "how possible it is for us to carry bread and meat to God's servants… and yet be ravens still!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill:** Notes the ravens brought "bread made and baked, and the flesh boiled, broiled, or roasted." Regarding the source, records a Jewish tradition that the food "was fetched from Ahab's table" or from the tables of the 7,000 faithful. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)

---

### v. 7 — The Brook Dries Up

**Traditional Reading:** After some time ("at the end of days" — possibly a year, per Gill), the brook dried up because of the very drought Elijah had prayed for. Elijah did not pray for rain even for his own survival — he kept God's purpose first.

— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Cites Meyer: "Ah, it is hard to sit beside a drying brook — much harder than to face the prophets of Baal on Carmel." Meyer lists different kinds of drying brooks believers face: popularity, health, money, friendship. "Why does God let them dry? He wants to teach us not to trust in His gifts but in Himself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill:** "After a while, or 'at the end of days,' perhaps a year, which sometimes is the sense of this phrase." Also notes the Phoenician historian Menander recorded a drought in the time of Ithobalus (Ethbaal, father of Jezebel) lasting a whole year. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Constable:** "Elijah was learning experientially that Yahweh was the only source of food." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)

---

### vv. 8–9 — Called to Zarephath of Sidon

**Traditional Reading:** God sends Elijah to Zarephath (between Tyre and Sidon), in the heartland of Baal worship — Jezebel's home territory. God says He has "commanded" a widow there to provide for him. This was a triple test: going to a Gentile city, to Baal's homeland, and to a widow (the poorest class).

— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "God kept transplanting Elijah: From home to Jezreel to Cherith to Zarephath." Widows "were notorious for their poverty." Jesus used this example to show God's right to choose a people for Himself (Luke 4:24–26). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill:** "This might be a trial of the prophet's faith, to be sent to dwell in a place belonging to the Zidonians, among whom Jezebel had an interest." On "I have commanded": "not that this was declared to the woman… but that he had determined it in his mind, and would take care in his providence." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Constable:** "The site of Zarephath was between Tyre and Sidon in Phoenicia, the stronghold of the cult that Ahab had imported into Israel." Notes F.C. Fensham: "In the absence of Baal who lies impotent in the Netherworld, Yahweh steps in to assist the widow and the orphan, and this is even done in the heartland of Baal, Phoenicia." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)
— **Bridgeway (non-denominational):** "The miraculous feeding… showed that God's power was greater than Baal's even in Baal's home country; and, unlike Baal's, it could work independently of nature." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/17-11.html)

---

### vv. 10–11 — Elijah Meets the Widow at the Gate

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah finds the widow gathering sticks — a sign of extreme poverty. He asks first for water, then for bread. The double request gradually reveals her desperate state and tests her hospitality.

— **Gill:** The widow "made no difficulty of granting his request." Elijah's further request for bread was "still further to try her whether she was the person that was to sustain him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Quotes Spurgeon: "You learn this from the fact that she had not even firewood. Now, there was no reason why she should not have had that even in time of famine of bread… unless she had been extremely poor." Also, the woman seemed unaware of God's command — "She does not appear to have been at all aware that she was to feed a prophet." God's unseen hand prepared her heart. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Constable:** "Elijah's request for water and then bread evidently identified the widow God had in mind (cf. Genesis 24:10–21)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)

---

### v. 12 — The Widow's Desperate Reply

**Traditional Reading:** The widow swears "As the LORD your God lives" — showing she recognizes Israel's God, yet as Elijah's God, not yet her own. She has only a handful of flour and a little oil, gathering sticks for a final meal for herself and her son, after which they will die.

— **Gill:** "Which shows her to be a good woman, swearing by the living God, and him only, and that she took Elijah to be a good man, and a prophet of the Lord." The phrase "two sticks" is a meiosis (understatement) — meaning a few sticks. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Notes the polite address "'As the LORD your God lives'… showed that she respected God, yet recognized that the God of Israel was Elijah's God and not her own." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian/Evangelical, via StudyLight):** Observes she "had no fuel but the sticks she gathered in the streets, and, having no servant, she must gather them herself, being thus more in a condition to receive alms than give entertainment." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/17-11.html)

---

### vv. 13–14 — Elijah's Bold Request and God's Promise

**Traditional Reading:** "Do not fear" is God's first word to her. Elijah asks her to make him a small cake *first*, then for herself and her son. The condition for blessing is putting God's interests (represented by the prophet) before her own. He promises the flour and oil will not run out until the drought ends.

— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "This was an audaciously bold request from the prophet… This seemed like the worst kind of predatory fund-raising." But the promise underpinned it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill:** "Which was not said from a selfish spirit of the prophet, but to try the faith of the woman… if she dressed it for herself and her son first, there would have been none left for the divine blessing to descend upon." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Matthew Henry (via StudyLight):** Calls this "as great a trial as could be in so small a matter." He marvels: "O woman! great was thy faith; one has not found the like, no, not in Israel: all things considered, it exceeded that of the widow who, when she had but two mites, cast them into the treasury." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/17-11.html)
— **Constable:** "Elijah asked the widow to put God's interests — represented by himself, a prophet of Yahweh — before her own as the condition for her blessing (cf. Matthew 6:33; Mark 12:41–44)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)

---

### vv. 15–16 — The Widow's Obedience and Ongoing Miracle

**Traditional Reading:** The widow obeyed, and the household ate for many days (possibly up to two years). The flour and oil never ran out. This was a continuous miracle of multiplication, not a one-time supply.

— **Gill:** "There being a continual increase and supply of both, through the mighty power of God working a continued miracle; just as the loaves and fishes were increased while the disciples were eating." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Quotes Spurgeon on why God didn't give a full granary: "In days of famine men are sharp of scent, and it would soon have been noised about the city… They would have caused a riot, and robbed the house, and perhaps, have killed the woman and her son." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Pulpit Commentary (Anglican):** Notes the miracle is "doubly remarkable" — first, God supplies "homely and trivial needs," and second, it is "a miracle of multiplication, which is virtual creation… doing rapidly and directly what, under ordinary laws, has to be done slowly." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/17.htm)

**Traditions Compared:** Some Word of Faith / prosperity teachers have used this passage to teach a "principle of first fruits" — give to the "man of God" first and God will multiply your resources. However, none of the traditional commentaries examined frame it this way; they universally see it as a test of faith particular to this moment of redemptive history, not a universal financial principle. (Note: I was unable to access direct Word of Faith sources due to search limits, but the traditional sources consistently interpret the passage Christologically and redemptive-historically, not as a formula for wealth.)

---

### vv. 17–18 — The Widow's Son Dies; Her Accusation

**Traditional Reading:** The son falls deathly ill and dies. The widow, in her grief, blames Elijah (indirectly) and her own sin (directly): "Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?" She assumes the presence of the holy prophet has brought divine judgment on her sin.

— **Gill:** "She said this rashly, and in her passion and agony, being extremely affected with the death of her child, which made her forget and overlook all the benefits she had received." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Notes this was "a double blow" — loss of a child and loss of her only hope for future provision. "Whatever her sin was, the guilty memory of it was always close to her." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Constable:** "The widow incorrectly blamed herself for her son's predicament (cf. John 9:2–3)." Also sees the sickness of the son as corresponding to "Israel's spiritual condition at this time." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)
— **Ellicott (Anglican):** Traces the widow's faith journey: first she spoke of "the LORD *your* God" (v. 12), then recognized Him as God at the death (v. 18), and after the resurrection declares full faith (v. 24). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/17.htm)

---

### vv. 19–20 — Elijah Takes the Child and Prays

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah takes the boy from his mother's arms, carries him to his upper room, lays him on his own bed, and cries out to God. His prayer expresses anguish: "Have You also brought tragedy on this widow who has opened her home to me?"

— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Elijah prayed with great heart and intimacy with God. He brought this seemingly unexplainable and irredeemable tragedy to God in prayer. Since he knew God led him to this widow, Elijah laid this tragedy on God and asked Him to remedy it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Gill:** "He pleads his interest in the Lord, and makes use of it as an argument with him to hear his prayer; he observes the character and condition of the woman, a widow… and he urges the kindness of her to him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)

---

### v. 21 — Stretching Out Over the Child Three Times

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah stretches himself over the child three times and prays for the soul (life) to return. This is the first resurrection recorded in Scripture.

— **Gill:** "Or 'measured himself' on it… putting his mouth on its mouth, his eyes on its eyes, his hands on its hands, as Elisha afterwards did (2 Kings 4:34), thereby showing his great affection to the child, and in order to increase it the more, and to make him the more fervent and importunate in his prayers for its life; and hereby signifying also that he would if he could infuse his breath and life into it, and warm it with his own heat." Gill also notes: "a proof this that the soul dies not with the body, but exists in a separate state without it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Ellicott / Pulpit (Anglican):** "To suppose that this implies merely the use of some natural means of reviving the dead, is simply to explain the whole description away. The idea… clearly is of a certain healing 'virtue,' attaching in measure to the person of the prophets, as without measure it belonged to our Lord Himself." Notes the power was conditional on prayer: "the Lord heard the voice of Elijah." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "This was an unusual prayer technique, but Elijah had no precedent for this. It was not because of his prayer technique, but because of his faith that God answered this prayer." Also rejects the Syriac/Jerome tradition that the boy was Jonah as "totally unsatisfactory and historically impossible." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-17/)
— **Constable:** "Often in cases of miraculous restoration, God's servant placed his hand on the afflicted one. He did so to indicate that the power of God in him was passing to the needy individual (cf. Matthew 8:3)." Calls this "the first restoration to life of a dead person that Scripture records." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)

---

### v. 22 — The LORD Heard and the Child Revived

**Traditional Reading:** God answers Elijah's prayer. The child's soul returns and he revives. This demonstrates Yahweh, not Baal, has power over life and death.

— **Gill:** "This is the first instance of anyone being raised from the dead; this Satan has imitated; hence the many fabulous stories with the Heathens of persons being raised to life after death." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Pulpit Commentary:** "And the soul of the child came into him again and he revived [or recovered. Cf. 2 Kings 1:2; 2 Kings 8:8]." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Bridgeway:** "The healing of the widow's son confirmed her faith in God, and assured Elijah of God's presence and power in the dangerous and lonely days ahead." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/17-11.html)

---

### v. 23 — Elijah Presents the Living Son

**Traditional Reading:** Elijah carries the living boy down and presents him to his mother with the simple declaration: "Look, your son is alive."

— **Gill:** "Being come to life, he took it off of the bed in his bedchamber, and brought it down to the lower part of the house, where the woman was." Notes Bunting says inhabitants of Zarephath still show the chamber where Elijah raised the child. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)

---

### v. 24 — The Widow's Confession of Faith

**Traditional Reading:** The widow declares full conviction: "Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth." This is the climax of her faith journey.

— **Ellicott (Anglican):** Traces the stages of her faith: (1) "the LORD *your* God" (v. 12) — distant; (2) recognition of Jehovah as God at the death (v. 18); (3) now full conviction and likely conversion. Compares to the nobleman of Capernaum (John 4:47, 50, 53). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Gill:** "She took him to be one at his first coming to her; she was in a great measure confirmed in it by the miracle of the barrel of meal and cruse of oil; but upon the death of her son, which she was ready to impute to the prophet, she was staggered at it; but now, by his resurrection from the dead, was fully assured of it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm)
— **Enduring Word / Constable:** Both note that the widow (a Gentile from Baal's heartland) becomes a witness that Yahweh's word is truth — a foreshadowing of Gentile inclusion. Constable: "The best proof of the effectiveness of Elijah's preparation is that he was verified as an authentic man of God… by a daughter of the very people he opposed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-17.html)
— **Precept Austin:** Notes that the theme of the chapter is that "the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth" — the reliability of God's word spoken through His prophet. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-17-commentary)

---

## Points Where Traditions Differ

### On the Ravens (v. 4, 6)

The vast majority of Protestant commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Guzik, Constable) affirm literal ravens as a miracle. The Pulpit Commentary explicitly rejects alternative readings (Arabs, merchants) as arising "simply from a desire to get rid of what seemed a strange miracle." No tradition examined argued for a non-miraculous interpretation. **I was unable to obtain modern scholarly or Catholic/Orthodox views on this point due to search limits.**

### On Elijah Stretching Over the Child (v. 21)

— **Gill (Baptist, older):** Sees it partly as expressing affection, partly as warming the body, and notes it as proof the soul exists apart from the body.
— **Ellicott / Pulpit (Anglican):** Sees a genuine "healing virtue" attached to the prophet's person — a mediated divine power, analogous to Christ's healing (Luke 8:45–46), but conditional on prayer.
— **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Dismisses the "technique" angle entirely — it was faith, not method, that God honored.
— **Constable (Dispensational):** Sees it as a symbolic act indicating that God's power in the prophet was passing to the needy individual (cf. Matthew 8:3; Acts 20:10).

These differences are largely in emphasis rather than contradiction: all agree the resurrection was a divine miracle in answer to prayer.

### On the Widow's Sin (v. 18)

— **Traditional Protestant:** The widow's cry reflects a common ancient Near Eastern belief that proximity to a holy man brings judgment on one's sins. Constable explicitly says she "incorrectly blamed herself" — the death was not punishment for a specific sin.
— **Reformed / Piper:** Would emphasize God's sovereignty even over tragedy, using it to deepen faith (the widow moved from "your God" to full confession).
— **Catholic/Orthodox view:** I was unable to access these sources due to search limits.

### On Prosperity/Word of Faith Use of vv. 13–16

I was unable to access direct Word of Faith sources. Traditional commentaries universally treat the promise of inexhaustible flour and oil as a unique redemptive-historical miracle authenticating Elijah's prophetic office and demonstrating Yahweh's superiority over Baal — not as a universal "give to get" principle.
